cards.q: Define relative molecular mass, \(M_{\text{r}}\).
cards.a: The weighted mean mass of a molecule of a compound compared with \(\frac{1}{12}\) of the mass of an atom of carbon-12.
cards.why: In practice it is found by adding up the relative atomic masses of all the atoms in the formula.

cards.q: Calculate the relative formula mass of hydrated copper(II) sulfate, \(\mathrm{CuSO_{4}{\cdot}5H_{2}O}\). (\(A_{\text{r}}\): Cu 63.5, S 32.1, O 16.0, H 1.0)
cards.why: The water of crystallisation is part of the formula, so its mass is included. “Formula mass” is used because the compound is ionic.

cards.q: What is the Avogadro constant?
cards.a: The number of particles in one mole of a substance: \(6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\).
cards.why: A mole of any substance contains the same number of particles (atoms, molecules, ions or electrons), so moles let chemists count particles by weighing.

cards.q: What is the unit of amount of substance, and what is molar mass?
cards.a: Amount of substance is measured in moles (mol). Molar mass is the mass per mole of a substance, in \(\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
cards.why: Molar mass has the same number as \(M_{\text{r}}\): \(M_{\text{r}}\) of water is 18.0, so its molar mass is \(18.0\ \text{g mol}^{-1}\).

cards.q: Write the equation linking amount of substance, mass and molar mass (or relative formula mass).
cards.why: The mass must be in grams; convert from kilograms or tonnes first.

cards.q: Calculate the amount, in mol, in 4.00 g of sodium hydroxide, \(\mathrm{NaOH}\). (\(A_{\text{r}}\): Na 23.0, O 16.0, H 1.0)
cards.why: Give the answer to the same number of significant figures as the data (3).

cards.q: Calculate the mass of 0.250 mol of calcium carbonate, \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}}\). (\(A_{\text{r}}\): Ca 40.1, C 12.0, O 16.0)
cards.why: Rearrange \(n = \frac{m}{M}\) to \(m = nM\).

cards.q: How many atoms are there in 9.00 g of water, \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\)? (\(M_{\text{r}} = 18.0\), \(L = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\))
cards.why: Read the question carefully: atoms, molecules and ions give different answers.

cards.q: How many ions are there in 5.85 g of sodium chloride? (\(M_{\text{r}}\) NaCl \(= 58.5\), \(L = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\))
steps: Each formula unit gives two ions, \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\): \(0.200\ \text{mol}\) of ions.
cards.why: The mole applies to any stated particle: here, ions.

cards.q: Calculate the mass, in grams, of one molecule of carbon dioxide. (\(M_{\text{r}} = 44.0\), \(L = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\))
steps: One mole (\(6.022 \times 10^{23}\) molecules) has a mass of 44.0 g.
cards.why: Divide the molar mass by the Avogadro constant to get the mass of one particle.

cards.q: Write the equation linking amount, concentration (in \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\)) and volume of a solution in \(\text{cm}^{3}\).
cards.a:
\(n = \frac{c \times V}{1000}\)
where \(V\) is in \(\text{cm}^{3}\). With \(V\) in \(\text{dm}^{3}\): \(n = cV\).
cards.why: \(1\ \text{dm}^{3} = 1000\ \text{cm}^{3}\), so divide a volume in \(\text{cm}^{3}\) by 1000 to get \(\text{dm}^{3}\).

cards.q: Calculate the amount of hydrochloric acid in 25.0 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) of a 0.100 \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\) solution.
cards.why: Forgetting to convert \(\text{cm}^{3}\) to \(\text{dm}^{3}\) makes the answer 1000 times too big.

cards.q: 2.65 g of anhydrous sodium carbonate, \(\mathrm{Na_{2}CO_{3}}\), is dissolved and made up to 250 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) in a volumetric flask. Calculate the concentration in \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\). (\(M_{\text{r}} = 106.0\))
cards.why: A solution of accurately known concentration like this is called a standard solution.

cards.q: Convert a sodium hydroxide concentration of 0.150 \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\) into \(\text{g dm}^{-3}\). (\(M_{\text{r}}\) NaOH \(= 40.0\))
steps: Mass \(= 0.150 \times 40.0 = 6.00\ \text{g}\), so the concentration is \(6.00\ \text{g dm}^{-3}\).
cards.why: Concentration in \(\text{g dm}^{-3}\) \(=\) concentration in \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\) \(\times\ M_{\text{r}}\).

cards.q: 25.0 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) of 2.00 \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\) sulfuric acid is diluted with water to 250 \(\text{cm}^{3}\). Calculate the new concentration.
steps: Dilution does not change the amount of acid.
cards.why: The volume increased ten times, so the concentration fell to one tenth.

cards.q: True or false: \(n = c \times V\) can be used with the volume in \(\text{cm}^{3}\).
cards.a: False. With \(c\) in \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\), \(V\) must be in \(\text{dm}^{3}\): divide \(\text{cm}^{3}\) by 1000.

cards.q: State the ideal gas equation and the SI unit of each quantity.
cards.a:
\(pV = nRT\)
\(p\): pressure in Pa
\(V\): volume in \(\text{m}^{3}\)
\(n\): amount in mol
\(R\): gas constant, \(8.31\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\)
\(T\): temperature in K
cards.why: Students are not expected to recall R; it is given. Getting the units right is where most marks are lost.

cards.q: Convert these into SI units for \(pV = nRT\): 250 \(\text{cm}^{3}\); 2.00 \(\text{dm}^{3}\); 101 kPa; 25 °C.
cards.why: \(1\ \text{cm}^{3} = 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^{3}\), \(1\ \text{dm}^{3} = 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^{3}\), \(1\ \text{kPa} = 10^{3}\ \text{Pa}\), and temperature in K \(=\) temperature in °C \(+\ 273\).

cards.q: Calculate the volume, in \(\text{dm}^{3}\), occupied by 0.500 mol of an ideal gas at 100 kPa and 298 K. (\(R = 8.31\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\))
cards.why: The equation gives \(V\) in \(\text{m}^{3}\); convert at the end if the question asks for \(\text{dm}^{3}\).

cards.q: 0.0200 mol of a gas occupies 500 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) at 150 kPa. Calculate its temperature in kelvin. (\(R = 8.31\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\))
cards.why: Rearrange first, then substitute values already in SI units.

cards.q: 0.362 g of a volatile liquid is vaporised. The vapour occupies 150 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) at 101 kPa and 373 K. Calculate the relative molecular mass of the liquid. (\(R = 8.31\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\))
cards.why: Keep unrounded values in the calculator until the final step.

cards.q: True or false: in \(pV = nRT\) you can use the temperature in °C, the pressure in kPa and the volume in \(\text{dm}^{3}\).
cards.a: False. Use SI units: K, Pa and \(\text{m}^{3}\).
cards.why: Using °C gives nonsense (at 0 °C the volume would come out as zero), and mixing kPa with \(\text{m}^{3}\) makes the answer 1000 times out.

cards.q: What is the molar volume of a gas at room temperature and pressure, and what does it allow you to do?
cards.why: One mole of any gas occupies the same volume at the same temperature and pressure; the value 24 applies only at room temperature and pressure.

cards.q: 5.00 g of calcium carbonate reacts with excess hydrochloric acid. Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide formed at room temperature and pressure. (\(M_{\text{r}}\) \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}} = 100.1\); molar volume \(= 24.0\ \text{dm}^{3}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\))
cards.why: The 1 : 1 ratio of \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}}\) to \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) comes from the balanced equation.

cards.q: 20 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) of propane burns completely: \(\mathrm{C_{3}H_{8}(g) + 5O_{2}(g) \rightarrow 3CO_{2}(g) + 4H_{2}O(l)}\). Calculate the volume of oxygen used and of carbon dioxide made, at the same temperature and pressure.
steps: Equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal amounts, so volume ratio \(=\) mole ratio.
cards.why: The water is a liquid at room temperature, so it does not count as a gas volume.

cards.q: Outline how the molar volume of a gas can be measured in the laboratory.
cards.a: React a weighed amount of a reactant (for example magnesium ribbon) with excess acid in a sealed flask. Collect the gas in a gas syringe or an inverted measuring cylinder of water and measure its volume. Calculate the amount of gas from the equation; molar volume \(=\) volume ÷ amount.
cards.why: The other reactant must be in excess so the weighed reactant reacts completely.

cards.q: 0.0360 g of magnesium reacts with excess hydrochloric acid and gives 36.0 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) of hydrogen at room temperature. Calculate the molar volume of hydrogen in \(\text{dm}^{3}\) \(\text{mol}^{-1}\). (\(A_{\text{r}}\) Mg \(= 24.3\))
cards.why: Compare it with the data-book value of 24 to judge the error.

cards.q: True or false: one mole of any gas always occupies 24 \(\text{dm}^{3}\).
cards.a: False. \(24\ \text{dm}^{3}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\) is the molar volume only at room temperature and pressure.
cards.why: Gas volume depends on temperature and pressure; under other conditions use \(pV = nRT\).

cards.q: Define empirical formula and molecular formula.
cards.a:
Empirical formula: the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
Molecular formula: the actual number of atoms of each element in a molecule.
cards.why: Ethene, \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{4}}\), has the empirical formula \(\mathrm{CH_{2}}\).

cards.q: A compound contains 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen by mass. Its \(M_{\text{r}}\) is 180. Find its empirical and molecular formulae. (\(A_{\text{r}}\): C 12.0, H 1.0, O 16.0)
steps: Divide by the smallest (3.33): C 1, H 2, O 1, so \(\mathrm{CH_{2}O}\).
cards.why: Glucose has this formula. Multiply every subscript in the empirical formula by the same whole number.

cards.q: 1.27 g of copper is heated in air until its mass is constant at 1.59 g. Find the empirical formula of the oxide. (\(A_{\text{r}}\): Cu 63.5, O 16.0)
cards.why: Heating to constant mass shows the reaction is complete.

cards.q: A hydrocarbon has the empirical formula \(\mathrm{CH_{2}}\) and \(M_{\text{r}} = 56.0\). What is its molecular formula?
cards.why: The molecular formula is always a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula.

cards.q: A gaseous hydrocarbon has the empirical formula \(\mathrm{CH_{2}}\). 0.210 g of it occupies 124 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) at 100 kPa and 298 K. Find its molecular formula. (\(R = 8.31\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\))
cards.why: The ideal gas equation gives the amount, and mass ÷ amount gives \(M_{\text{r}}\).

cards.q: 2.46 g of hydrated magnesium sulfate, \(\mathrm{MgSO_{4}{\cdot}xH_{2}O}\), is heated to constant mass, leaving 1.20 g of anhydrous \(\mathrm{MgSO_{4}}\). Find \(x\). (\(M_{\text{r}}\): \(\mathrm{MgSO_{4}}\) 120.4, \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\) 18.0)
cards.why: This is Epsom salts, \(\mathrm{MgSO_{4}{\cdot}7H_{2}O}\). Round to the nearest whole number only at the end.

cards.q: When finding the water of crystallisation in a hydrated salt by heating, why must the salt be heated to constant mass, and what error results if it is not?
cards.a: Constant mass shows all the water has been driven off.
marks: Heat, cool and weigh repeatedly until two readings agree.
If some water remains, the mass of water lost is too small.
So the calculated value of \(x\) is too low.

cards.q: Balance the equation for the complete combustion of butane, including state symbols.
cards.why: Balance C, then H, then O last. Halves are allowed while working (\(6\tfrac{1}{2}\ \mathrm{O_{2}}\)), then double everything.

cards.q: Iron(III) oxide is reduced by carbon monoxide to iron and carbon dioxide. Write the balanced equation.
cards.why: Each CO takes one oxygen atom from the oxide, so three CO are needed for Fe₂O₃.

cards.q: What is an ionic equation, and what are spectator ions?
cards.a: An ionic equation shows only the species that take part in the reaction. Spectator ions are present in the solution but are unchanged, so they are left out.
cards.why: In \(\mathrm{HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq)}\), \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) are spectator ions.

cards.q: Write the ionic equation for the neutralisation of any strong acid by any alkali.
cards.why: All the other ions are spectators, so every strong acid–alkali neutralisation has the same ionic equation.

cards.q: Marble chips react with dilute hydrochloric acid. Give the ionic equation, with state symbols, and two observations.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}(s) + 2H^{+}(aq) \rightarrow Ca^{2+}(aq) + H_{2}O(l) + CO_{2}(g)}\)
Observations: effervescence (fizzing); the solid gets smaller and disappears.
cards.why: \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}}\) is insoluble, so it is written in full as a solid, not as separate ions.

cards.q: Silver nitrate solution is added to sodium chloride solution. Give the ionic equation and the observation.
cards.why: \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\) and \(\mathrm{NO_{3}^{-}}\) are spectator ions.

cards.q: Zinc powder is added to blue copper(II) sulfate solution. Give the ionic equation and two observations.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{Zn(s) + Cu^{2+}(aq) \rightarrow Zn^{2+}(aq) + Cu(s)}\)
The blue colour fades to colourless; a pink-brown solid forms (and the mixture warms).
cards.why: Zinc is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from its ions.

cards.q: Calculate the mass of calcium oxide formed when 10.0 g of calcium carbonate is completely decomposed: \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}(s) \rightarrow CaO(s) + CO_{2}(g)}\). (\(M_{\text{r}}\): \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}}\) 100.1, CaO 56.1)
cards.why: Mass → moles, use the ratio from the equation, then moles → mass.

cards.q: Calculate the maximum mass of iron, in tonnes, that can be made from 1.00 tonne of iron(III) oxide: \(\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3} + 3CO \rightarrow 2Fe + 3CO_{2}}\). (\(A_{\text{r}}\): Fe 55.8, O 16.0)
cards.why: Shortcut check: \(\frac{2 \times 55.8}{159.6} = 0.699\) of the oxide’s mass is iron.

cards.q: 2.43 g of magnesium is added to 50.0 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) of 1.00 \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\) hydrochloric acid. Which reagent is in excess, and what amount of hydrogen forms? (\(A_{\text{r}}\) Mg \(= 24.3\))
cards.a: Magnesium is in excess; 0.0250 mol of hydrogen forms.
steps: 0.100 mol Mg needs 0.200 mol HCl, but only 0.0500 mol is present, so HCl limits.
cards.why: The amount of product is set by the limiting reagent, not by the one in excess.

cards.q: How is percentage yield calculated?
cards.a: \(\text{percentage yield} = \frac{\text{actual mass of product}}{\text{theoretical (maximum) mass of product}} \times 100\)
cards.why: Amounts in moles can be used instead of masses, as long as top and bottom match.

cards.q: Heating 10.0 g of calcium carbonate should give 5.60 g of calcium oxide, but a student obtains 4.80 g. Calculate the percentage yield.
cards.why: The theoretical yield always comes from the balanced equation and the limiting reagent.

cards.q: Give reasons why the percentage yield of a reaction is usually less than 100%.
cards.a: Product is not formed or is lost.
marks: The reaction may be reversible or incomplete.
Side reactions may make other products.
Product is lost when it is separated or purified (filtering, transferring, recrystallising).

cards.q: How is percentage atom economy calculated?
cards.a: \(\text{atom economy} = \frac{M_{\text{r}}\ \text{of desired product}}{\text{sum of}\ M_{\text{r}}\ \text{of all reactants}} \times 100\)
cards.why: Use the balanced equation, multiplying each \(M_{\text{r}}\) by its coefficient. The sum for all reactants equals the sum for all products.

aqa.note: AQA writes the bottom line as the sum of the molecular masses of all reactants.

edexcel.note: Edexcel writes the bottom line as the sum of the molar masses of all products; the value is the same.

cards.q: Ethanol can be made by fermentation, \(\mathrm{C_{6}H_{12}O_{6} \rightarrow 2C_{2}H_{5}OH + 2CO_{2}}\), or by hydrating ethene, \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{4} + H_{2}O \rightarrow C_{2}H_{5}OH}\). Calculate the atom economy of fermentation. (\(M_{\text{r}}\): glucose 180.0, ethanol 46.0)
cards.why: In fermentation almost half the mass is lost as \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\); an addition reaction has only one product, so its atom economy is 100%.

cards.q: Calculate the atom economy for making iron by \(\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3} + 3CO \rightarrow 2Fe + 3CO_{2}}\). (\(M_{\text{r}}\): \(\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}}\) 159.6, CO 28.0; \(A_{\text{r}}\) Fe 55.8)
cards.why: Check: products \(111.6 + (3 \times 44.0) = 243.6\), the same total.

cards.q: Explain the advantages to industry and society of developing processes with a high atom economy.
cards.a: Less of the starting material ends up as waste.
marks: Economic: more of the raw materials become saleable product, so costs are lower.
Less waste to separate, treat or dispose of, which also costs money.
Environmental: less waste and pollution, and finite raw materials last longer.
Ethical: more sustainable use of resources for future generations.

cards.q: True or false: a reaction with a 95% yield must have a high atom economy.
cards.a: False. Yield and atom economy measure different things.
cards.why: Yield compares the product obtained with the maximum possible; atom economy depends only on the equation, i.e. how much of the reactants’ mass can ever end up in the desired product.

cards.q: Describe how to make up 250 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) of a standard solution from a solid.
cards.a: Weigh the solid accurately; dissolve it in a little distilled water in a beaker; transfer the solution to a 250 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) volumetric flask, rinsing the beaker and funnel into the flask; make up to the mark with distilled water so the bottom of the meniscus is on the line; stopper and invert to mix.
cards.why: The rinsings make sure all the solid reaches the flask, so the concentration is exactly known.

cards.q: Give the key steps in carrying out an accurate acid–base titration.
cards.a: Rinse the pipette and burette with the solutions they will hold. Pipette a measured volume into a conical flask and add a few drops of indicator. Fill the burette, removing the air bubble below the tap. Add from the burette while swirling, dropwise near the end point, over a white tile. Read the burette at eye level from the bottom of the meniscus. Repeat until titres are concordant.
cards.why: Rinsing with water instead would dilute the solution and change its concentration.

cards.q: Give the colour change at the end point when (a) phenolphthalein and (b) methyl orange is used, with acid added from the burette to alkali.
cards.a:
(a) Phenolphthalein: pink to colourless.
(b) Methyl orange: yellow to orange.
cards.why: Phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in alkali; methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in alkali, orange at the end point.

cards.q: Titres of 24.10 (rough), 23.45, 23.95, 23.50 and 23.40 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) are recorded. Which should be used to calculate the mean titre, and what is it?
cards.a:
Use the concordant titres, within 0.10 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) of each other: 23.45, 23.50 and 23.40.
Mean \(= 23.45\ \text{cm}^{3}\).
cards.why: The rough titre and the outlier (23.95) are left out.

cards.q: 25.0 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) of sodium hydroxide solution is neutralised by 22.50 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) of 0.100 \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\) hydrochloric acid. Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide.
cards.why: Moles of the known solution → ratio → moles of the unknown → concentration.

cards.q: 25.0 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) of sodium hydroxide is neutralised by 20.00 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) of 0.0500 \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\) sulfuric acid. Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide.
cards.why: Sulfuric acid is diprotic, so the 1 : 2 ratio matters.

cards.q: An indigestion tablet containing calcium carbonate is added to 50.0 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) of 1.00 \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\) HCl (an excess). The leftover acid needs 30.0 \(\text{cm}^{3}\) of 1.00 \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\) NaOH. Calculate the mass of \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}}\) in the tablet. (\(M_{\text{r}} = 100.1\))
steps: HCl added: \(1.00 \times 0.0500 = 0.0500\ \text{mol}\); HCl left over \(= n(\mathrm{NaOH}) = 0.0300\ \text{mol}\)
HCl that reacted with the tablet \(= 0.0500 - 0.0300 = 0.0200\ \text{mol}\)
cards.why: This is a back titration: an insoluble solid cannot be titrated directly, so you measure the acid it did not use.

cards.q: A burette reads to ±0.05 \(\text{cm}^{3}\). What is the uncertainty in a titre, and the percentage uncertainty in a titre of 23.45 \(\text{cm}^{3}\)?
steps: A titre uses two readings (start and end), each ±0.05: total ±0.10 \(\text{cm}^{3}\).
cards.why: Uncertainties add when a value comes from the difference of two readings.

cards.q: A mass of 1.20 g is found by difference using a balance that reads to ±0.005 g. Calculate the percentage uncertainty.
cards.why: Weighing by difference means two readings, so double the uncertainty of one reading.

cards.q: How can the percentage uncertainty in a titration or weighing be reduced?
cards.a: Make the measured quantity larger, or use more precise apparatus.
marks: Use a larger mass of solid, or a larger volume, so the fixed uncertainty is a smaller fraction of the value.
For a titration, use concentrations that give a larger titre.
Use apparatus with a smaller uncertainty, such as a balance reading to more decimal places.

cards.q: What is the difference between a systematic error and a random error? Give an example of each.
cards.a:
Systematic error: shifts every result the same way, e.g. reading the top instead of the bottom of the meniscus every time.
Random error: unpredictable scatter, e.g. judging the end point slightly differently each time.
cards.why: Repeats and averaging reduce random error but not systematic error.

cards.q: An experiment gives the molar volume of a gas as 23.1 \(\text{dm}^{3}\) \(\text{mol}^{-1}\); the accepted value is 24.0. Calculate the percentage error and suggest a source of error.
cards.a: 3.8%; for example, gas escapes before the bung is replaced.
cards.why: A low volume means gas was lost or not all collected; some hydrogen or carbon dioxide may also dissolve in water.

cards.q: To how many significant figures should a calculated answer be given?
cards.a: To the same number as the least precise piece of data used.
cards.why: A result can only be as precise as the least accurate measurement. Keep extra figures in the working and round only at the end.

cards.q: What is the difference between a hazard and a risk? Give a precaution when using 2 \(\text{mol dm}^{-3}\) sodium hydroxide.
cards.a:
Hazard: something that could cause harm (sodium hydroxide is corrosive).
Risk: the chance of harm happening and how serious it would be.
Precaution: wear eye protection (goggles) and wash spills off skin at once.
cards.why: Precautions reduce the risk; they do not remove the hazard.
